title: Why board games are back
text: A few years ago, many people would have predicted the slow death of the board game. Why would anybody sit around a table with a box of cardboard pieces when a phone can offer a thousand games in a pocket? And yet, in cafés and living rooms across the world, dice are being rolled and cards are being dealt more eagerly than at any time in recent memory. Shop owners say that tabletop games are selling faster than they have for years.

Several reasons are usually mentioned. The first is simple fatigue. After a day spent looking at screens for school or work, many people feel an urge to do something with their hands, face to face with other human beings. A board game offers exactly that: a clear goal, a reason to talk and, at its best, plenty of laughter. Parents of teenagers sometimes report that a game is the only activity everyone at home agrees on. Nobody can scroll through a feed while waiting for a turn without annoying everybody else. Several players say that the physical pieces matter too: moving a wooden figure or holding a handful of cards feels more satisfying than touching a glass screen.

The games themselves have also changed. Classic titles that depend mostly on luck, in which players roll a dice and move along a path, have been joined by thousands of newer designs. Some ask players to cooperate against the game itself, some tell a story over several evenings, and others reward careful planning more than lucky throws. As a result, there is now a game for almost every temperament, from the competitive to the dreamy. A single title may even come with one version for two players and another for twelve. Designers have drawn on history, science and even cooking for ideas, and the best games can be explained in ten minutes yet remain interesting for years.

Board game cafés illustrate the trend. Customers pay a small fee, choose a game from a shelf of hundreds and are often helped by a member of staff who explains the rules. For many visitors, this removes the main obstacle to trying something new: the fear of spending an evening reading a thick instruction booklet. The staff are often enthusiasts themselves, and a good recommendation can turn a hesitant visitor into a regular. The cafés have also become a meeting place for people who might never have met otherwise, regardless of age. Some even hold quiet evenings for beginners, when experienced players help newcomers through their first game without competing seriously.

Teachers and psychologists have noticed other benefits. Players learn to lose with good grace, to negotiate and to think several moves ahead. Some language teachers use games to get shy students talking, because the rules provide a script of sorts and the pressure of speaking is lifted. None of this proves that games make people cleverer, as some enthusiasts claim, but the evidence that they improve social skills is encouraging. Players also discover how differently the same person can behave when something is at stake, which is useful to know about oneself.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics note that the hobby can be expensive, with some elaborate games costing as much as a pair of trainers, and that a collection soon outgrows the shelf. Others complain that groups of friends find it hard to agree on a time to meet, and a few players confess that they take the competition too seriously and have to remind themselves that it is only a game. Yet even the sceptics admit that something valuable is at stake: an evening in which the devices are put away and the main attraction is each other's company.

questions.q: The author begins by saying that …
options: board games were never really popular.
phones have made board games cheaper.
people used to play games more often.
the revival of board games was unexpected.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why do people turn to board games?
options: They want to impress their colleagues.
They need a change from screens.
They are bored with their usual friends.
They believe games improve concentration.

questions.q: The word reward in paragraph 3 most probably means …
options: pay.
praise.
favour.
punish.

questions.q: In paragraph 4, what does 'this' in 'this removes the main obstacle to trying something new' refer to?
options: Customers being helped by staff who explain the rules.
Paying a small fee for the use of a game.
Selecting a title from the hundreds on display.
Meeting people of a different age.

questions.q: Which benefit of board games is NOT mentioned in paragraph 5?
options: Raising children's school marks.
Practising negotiation.
Helping shy students to speak.
Learning to accept defeat.

questions.q: What is the author's attitude to the claim that games make people cleverer?
options: Approving.
Curious.
Dismissive.
Sceptical.
board games are too expensive to be popular.
sceptics are wrong about the value of games.
the greatest value of games lies in being together.
screens should be banned from social events.
